parts: Lesson 21: Reproduction and Population Control — Summary

Asexual reproduction: a single parent, no gametes (bacteria, protista, lower plants and animals). Sexual reproduction: formation and fusion of gametes (fertilisation) giving a zygote. Gemmule: an asexual reproductive body of fresh water sponges, a tiny hard ball of undifferentiated cells (archaeocytes) covered by a resistant coat of chitin and spicules with a micropyle; it tides over unfavourable conditions (drying of ponds, winter) and the archaeocytes come out through the micropyle to form a new sponge. In insects sexes are usually separate; aphids reproduce parthenogenetically (all females). Cockroach: male has a pair of testes, vasa deferentia, ejaculatory duct, seminal vesicles, mushroom gland and gonapophyses; female has a pair of ovaries with ovarioles, oviducts, vagina, spermatheca (receives sperms), genital pouch and collaterial glands that form the ootheca (egg case).

Puberty is the period of maturation of sex organs and secondary sexual characters (males: deepening voice, beard, muscles; females: widening of pelvis, breasts, menstruation); adolescence is 10-19 years (WHO). Testes: extra-abdominal in the scrotum, which keeps the temperature 2-3 degrees Celsius lower than body temperature, suitable for sperm formation; each testis has coiled seminiferous tubules (sperm formation, spermatogenesis) and interstitial (Leydig) cells secreting testosterone. Epididymis stores sperms (viable but immotile); vas deferens carries sperms to the urethra; the urethra carries semen and urine; the penis is the copulatory organ. Accessory glands: seminal vesicles (nourishing fluid, 40-80 per cent of semen), prostate (alkaline fluid, activates sperms) and Cowper's glands (lubricating mucus). A sperm has a head with the acrosome (helps penetrate the egg), neck with centriole, middle piece with mitochondria and a tail (flagellum).

A pair of ovaries (produce ova, oestrogen and progesterone; oogenesis; follicle stages: primary follicle, Graafian follicle which ruptures at ovulation, leaving the corpus luteum), a pair of oviducts or Fallopian tubes (site of fertilisation; funnel-shaped infundibulum), uterus (pear-shaped; layers endometrium, myometrium and perimetrium; the embryo implants in it), vagina (birth canal) and external genitalia. Menstrual cycle (about 28 days): menstruation (days 1-4, shedding of the uterine lining); follicular phase (days 5-13; Graafian follicle matures and secretes oestrogen, which builds the endometrium); ovulation (13th-14th day; ovum released); luteal phase (corpus luteum secretes progesterone); if no fertilisation, the corpus luteum degenerates and the lining is shed on about the 28th day. Menarche is the onset of menstruation (11-13 years) and menopause is the stoppage (45-50 years). In pregnancy menstruation and ovulation stop because progesterone is secreted by the corpus luteum and then the placenta.

Sperms stay viable in the female tract for 24-72 hours; fertilisation occurs in the oviduct; the zygote divides to form a morula (day 4), then a blastocyst (day 5), which implants in the uterine wall about a week after fertilisation (embryo to pregnancy). Embryo development: zygote, morula, blastocyst, implantation; foetus with human features by 6 weeks; birth after about 40 weeks. Placenta: an association between maternal and foetal tissue where oxygen and nutrients pass from the mother to the foetus and CO2 and wastes pass back; it is permeable to gases, nutrients and antibodies, does not allow most germs (HIV can pass), and secretes progesterone and hCG. Umbilical cord: blood vascular connection between the foetus and the placenta. Amnion: a sac filled with amniotic fluid that acts as a shock absorber. Oxytocin from the posterior pituitary causes uterine contractions for childbirth; labour; the amnion bursts, the baby is expelled, the cord is tied and cut.

Lactation: secretion of milk by mammary glands, stimulated by prolactin (anterior pituitary) and ejected by oxytocin (posterior pituitary). Colostrum is the first thick yellowish milk, rich in proteins and fats and containing antibodies (IgA) which give passive immunity to the newborn; so a mother should feed the baby just after birth. Twins: fraternal (two ova fertilised by two sperms; may be of different sexes) and identical (one zygote divides into two separate embryos; same sex); Siamese twins are identical twins that fail to separate. New techniques: test tube baby (IVF: ova fertilised outside and the embryo placed in the uterus), artificial insemination (stored semen introduced at ovulation) and fertility drugs (FSH to stimulate follicles).

Terms: population density (individuals per sq km), birth rate or natality (live births per 1000 per year), death rate or mortality (deaths per 1000 per year), growth rate (birth rate minus death rate), census (official count). India's population was 23.8 crore in 1901 and 102.7 crore in 2001. Causes of growth: advances in agriculture and medicine, customs, illiteracy, economic reasons, desire for a male child, industrialisation. Problems: poor health, housing and education for the family; for the country, urbanisation and slums, pollution, pressure on food, water, minerals and energy. Population control: education, rhythm (safe period) method, condoms and diaphragms, intrauterine devices (copper T), oral pills, vasectomy and tubectomy (surgical), and medical termination of pregnancy (MTP) under medical supervision.
